title: [DevTools] Fix Fabric host-instance map leak when public instances are created lazily
body:
## Summary

In React Native's Fabric renderer, a host instance is a `{node, canonical}` wrapper whose `canonical.publicInstance` is created lazily. The DevTools backend keyed `publicInstanceToDevToolsInstanceMap` by `getPublicInstance(hostInstance)`, which returns the wrapper before lazy creation and the public instance after. So when an acquire ran before the public instance existed and the release ran after, the two used different keys, the release missed, and unmounted instances (with their Fibers) were retained indefinitely.

This change keys the map by the stable `canonical` object instead, through a new `getHostInstanceKey()` helper in `DevToolsNativeHost.js`. Public instances passed back in via `getElementIDForHostInstance`, `getSuspenseNodeIDForHostInstance`, and `getNearestMountedDOMNode` are normalized through `__internalInstanceHandle.stateNode.canonical` to the same key. Paper (`_nativeTag`) and DOM (identity) keying are unchanged.

Fixes #37752.

## How did you test this change?

- Reproduced the reported acquire/release key mismatch against current `main` with the real `getPublicInstance` code, simulating RN's lazy `canonical.publicInstance` creation: the release lookup missed before the fix and hits after it.
- Added `packages/react-devtools-shared/src/__tests__/hostInstanceMapKey-test.js` covering the mismatch repro, stable canonical keying before/after lazy public instance creation, public-instance lookup normalization, and unchanged Paper/DOM key behavior.

Note: I could not run `yarn test` locally because dependency installation fails on this machine's network, so I verified against the real module code directly; the new test is included for CI.

title: Fix react-hooks/refs false positive when comparing (not calling) ref-accessing functions
body:
## Summary

Closes #37521.

The `react-hooks/refs` rule (implemented by `validateNoRefAccessInRender` in `babel-plugin-react-compiler`) reported "Cannot access refs during render" when code merely *referenced* a function that accesses refs, without calling it:

```tsx
const sampleFunc = useCallback(() => {
  setSampleValue(++sampleRef.current);
}, []);
if (sampleFunc !== prevSampleFunc) { // <- false positive here
  ...
}
```

Comparing two function values never invokes either function, so no ref is actually accessed during render.

## Root cause

In the `BinaryExpression` case of `validateNoRefAccessInRenderImpl`, each operand was checked with `validateNoRefValueAccess`, which treats *any mention* of a function with a ref-reading effect (`Structure` type with `fn.readRefEffect`) as a ref access. That over-approximation is correct for call positions (handled separately: calling such a function during render errors via the `CallExpression` branch, and passing one to an unknown function errors via `validateNoRefPassedToFunction`), but not for binary operators, which never invoke their operands.

## Change

The `BinaryExpression` case now validates operands with `validateNoDirectRefValueAccess` instead, so genuine ref reads (e.g. `ref.current !== 5`) still error, while mere references to ref-accessing functions (e.g. `fn !== prevFn`) no longer do. The `if (ref.current == null)` guard pattern is unaffected.

## How did you test this change?

- Added fixture `allow-compare-ref-accessing-function-in-render.js` covering the reported pattern (comparing a ref-accessing function in render).
- Verified the TypeScript source parses cleanly (tsc, zero diagnostics).
- Audited all 17 existing fixtures that expect "Cannot access ref value during render": none exercise a binary comparison of ref-accessing functions (their comparisons are all direct `ref.current` reads, which still error), so no existing expectations change. The change strictly removes false-positive errors and cannot introduce new ones.

[DevTools] Fabric host-instance map misses releases when public instances are created lazily
body:
## Summary

React DevTools can retain unmounted React Native Fabric host instances indefinitely in `publicInstanceToDevToolsInstanceMap`. This is reproducible in an iOS Debug app using Hermes and Fabric, including when no DevTools frontend is attached.

## Root cause

The backend tracks a host instance by `getPublicInstance(hostInstance)` during both acquire and release:

- [`DevToolsNativeHost.js`, `getPublicInstance`](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/1d34f91dfde6bba84d08b683aaba164c7194dacb/packages/react-devtools-shared/src/backend/DevToolsNativeHost.js#L24-L49)
- [`fiber/renderer.js`, `aquireHostInstance` and `releaseHostInstance`](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/1d34f91dfde6bba84d08b683aaba164c7194dacb/packages/react-devtools-shared/src/backend/fiber/renderer.js#L295-L320)

Fabric lazily initializes `canonical.publicInstance` in React Native's `ReactFabric-dev.js:getPublicInstance`. Before that happens, the backend's helper falls back to using the `{node, canonical}` host wrapper as the key. After lazy initialization, a subsequent release uses the public instance instead, so `Map.get()` misses and the old key continues to retain the DevTools instance and Fiber subtree. Persistent mode also clones wrappers while sharing `canonical`, so wrapper identity is not a stable substitute.

## Minimal repro

1. Run a React Native Fabric Debug app with React DevTools enabled.
2. Mount a `<View>` without first reading its public instance. DevTools acquires the host instance while `canonical.publicInstance` is `null`.
3. After mount, attach a ref and call `ref.current.measure(...)` (or otherwise cause Fabric to lazily create its public instance).
4. Unmount the view.
5. Observe that `publicInstanceToDevToolsInstanceMap` still contains the entry keyed by the former `{node, canonical}` wrapper, retaining the unmounted DevTools instance/Fiber.

## Evidence

In an iOS Debug Hermes session on React Native Fabric, one lesson Continue→Next transition yielded 141 gets, 133 deletes, and 8 missed releases (5 wrapper-key misses and 3 public-instance-key misses). Across repeated cycles, we found 1,065 keys whose Fabric canonical was absent from every mounted Fiber root. Removing only those stale entries shrank the map by 1,065 and reduced heap-graph self bytes by about 22 MB. These heap measurements were after forced GC; Runtime console entries were cleared before snapshots and the pending initial-operation queue was flushed once when no frontend was attached.

## Suggested fix

Use the stable Fabric `canonical` object as the key for host-instance acquire and release. Normalize a public instance used by `getElementIDForHostInstance`/`getNearestMountedDOMNode` back to the same key via `publicInstance.__internalInstanceHandle.stateNode.canonical`. Keep current behavior for Paper and DOM. A renderer-injected identity callback would avoid hard-coding Fabric internals if the reconciler interface should own this distinction.

The exact issue has been checked in `react/react` and `react/react-native`; we commented on the closest related existing report, [PR #30831](https://github.com/react/react/pull/30831#issuecomment-5975797101), rather than duplicate its host-instance-map history. This report covers the distinct lazy-publicInstance key mismatch.

title: [DOM] Fix repeated Fragment focus() moving focus inside a ShadowRoot
body:
## Summary

Inside a ShadowRoot, calling `FragmentInstance.focus()` a second time moves focus to the next focusable child instead of leaving it where it is. `focusLast()` does the same in reverse:

```js
// Rendered into a ShadowRoot:
// <Fragment ref={ref}><button id="a" /><button id="b" /></Fragment>
ref.current.focus(); // focuses #a
ref.current.focus(); // focuses #b, should stay on #a
```

`setFocusIfFocusable()` short-circuits when the element already has focus, because `.focus()` on it fires no focus event and the element would otherwise read as unfocusable. It checked `element.ownerDocument.activeElement`, which inside a shadow tree is retargeted to the shadow host and never matches. It now compares against the root the element belongs to. #37615 fixes the same retargeting in `blur()`.

## How did you test this change?

The first commit adds tests that call `focus()` and `focusLast()` twice inside a ShadowRoot and capture the current behavior. The second commit has the fix and flips the assertions; they fail without the source change. `ReactDOMTestSelectors-test.js`, the other caller of `setFocusIfFocusable()`, still passes.

title: [Compiler] Fix use-before-initialization crash in the snap runner's non-watch mode
body:
## Summary

The `snap` fixture runner (`compiler/packages/snap`) crashed with a `ReferenceError` instead of reporting its result when run in non-watch mode (the mode used by `yarn workspace babel-plugin-react-compiler test` and the compiler CI workflow).

In `runTestCommand()`, the non-watch path does:

```ts
const tsWatch = watchSrc(
  () => {},
  async (isTypecheckSuccess) => {
    ...
    tsWatch?.close();   // <- read of the binding being initialized
    ...
  },
);
```

`watchSrc()` calls `ts.createWatchProgram()`, whose `afterProgramCreate` hook fires **synchronously, before the `watchSrc(...)` call returns** — i.e. before `tsWatch` is initialized. The completion callback therefore runs while `tsWatch` is still in its temporal dead zone.

On the type-check *success* path this is masked by the `await runFixtures(...)` before the `close()` call (the assignment completes during the await). But on the type-check *failure* path there is no `await` before `tsWatch?.close()`, so the runner crashes:

```
Found typescript errors in Forget source code, skipping test fixtures.

ReferenceError: Cannot access 'tsWatch' before initialization
    at D:\...\compiler\packages\snap\dist\runner.js:141:17
```

swallowing the real outcome (a failed type-check that should exit 1) in a confusing crash.

## The fix

Route the `close()` call through a `tsWatchRef` variable that is declared and initialized **before** `watchSrc()` is called and pointed at the returned watch right after it returns. The callback now reads `tsWatchRef?.close()` — safe on both the synchronous failure path (no-op, the process exits immediately afterwards) and the asynchronous success path (the watch is closed as before). The change is confined to the non-watch branch of `runTestCommand`; watch mode is untouched.

## How did you test this change?

Reproduced deterministically on the unfixed code, then re-ran the same steps with the fix (`node dist/main.js test -p <pattern>` from `compiler/packages/snap` after `yarn workspace snap run build`):

1. **Failure path** — temporarily added a type error to `packages/babel-plugin-react-compiler/src/index.ts` (`const x: number = 'no';`) and ran the non-watch runner:
   - before the fix: reports the TS error, prints `Found typescript errors in Forget source code, skipping test fixtures.`, then crashes with `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'tsWatch' before initialization`.
   - after the fix: reports the TS error, prints the same message, and exits with code **1** — no `ReferenceError` (verified `grep -c ReferenceError` → 0).
   - the temporary type error was reverted afterwards.
2. **Success path** — with clean sources, the runner type-checks, builds the compiler (`Built compiler successfully with tsup`), and runs the filtered fixtures end-to-exactly as before; `close()` is still reached via the async path (the `tsWatchRef` is assigned by the time the awaited fixture run completes).
3. `yarn workspace snap run build` (tsc) passes, and the file is Prettier-clean.

Note: on a Windows checkout the fixture *snapshots* themselves compare with CRLF vs LF noise in the generated markdown (working-tree line endings); this is environmental and unrelated to this change — the fixture run logic is exercised identically.

title: [Perf Track] Don't re-diff the same value pair when it is aliased under multiple props
body:
## Summary

Fixes #37628.

In development builds, the Component Performance Track records which props changed on each render by deep-diffing the previous and next props in `addObjectDiffToProperties()` (`packages/shared/ReactPerformanceTrackProperties.js`).

The diff keeps no record of object pairs it has already visited. When a prop object exposes the same underlying data under several names — a common shape in data-table and ORM-style libraries — the identical `(prev, next)` pair is re-diffed in full for every alias name, even though the aliases add no new objects. The cost therefore scales **linearly with the number of aliases**:

| alias names | entries per measure (reported) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 129.0 |
| 4 | 500.3 |
| 13 | 1560.4 |

(the reported app sustained ~1.9M entries/second over 15 minutes of dev profiling). The depth cap (`indent < 3` in the value walk) bounds depth only, not breadth, so it does not deduplicate shared subtrees.

## The fix

`addObjectDiffToProperties()` now tracks the `(prev, next)` object pairs it has already diffed for the update (a `WeakMap<Object, Set<Object>>`, so nothing is retained) and passes the set through the recursion. A repeated pair is noted with a single line — `Repeats a value pair already shown; the diff is omitted.` — instead of re-walking the subtree. This is safe because a repeated pair is identical by reference to a pair whose deep-equality result has already been accounted for in the diff.

In the shape from the issue, 13 aliases now produce one walk of the shared data instead of thirteen. The change is dev-only (the entire diff is `__DEV__`-gated) and does not alter what is reported for non-aliased props.

## How did you test this change?

Added a regression test in `packages/react-reconciler/src/__tests__/ReactPerformanceTrack-test.js` (same harness as the existing diff tests): a component whose single `aliases` prop exposes one 10-row array under three names (`a`, `b`, `c`), re-rendered with a fresh instance. The exact recorded `properties` are asserted:

- with the fix: the 10 rows' `tick` changes are emitted **once**, and `b` / `c` get the single `Repeats a value pair already shown; the diff is omitted.` marker (8 tests pass);
- without the fix (source change temporarily reverted, test kept): the new test fails because the row diff is emitted three times.

Verification:

- `yarn test ReactPerformanceTrack` (dev): `8 passed, 8 total` — including the pre-existing diff tests (`bails out of diffing wide arrays`, `diffs HTML-like objects`, deeply-equal hint, etc.), so non-aliased diff output is unchanged.
- `yarn test --prod ReactPerformanceTrack`: `8 passed, 8 total`.
- `yarn prettier`, `yarn linc` (lint on changed files), Flow (`dom-node` renderer): all clean.

title: [DevTools] Resolve MemoComponent wrappers in inspectHooksOfFiber
body:
## Summary

Fixes #37733.

When "Record why each component rendered while profiling" is enabled, the DevTools backend records a change description for every rendered component via `getChangeDescription()` in `backend/fiber/renderer.js`. For the function-component family of tags — including `MemoComponent` — it calls `inspectHooks(prevFiber)` / `inspectHooks(nextFiber)`.

`inspectHooksOfFiberImpl()` in `packages/react-debug-tools/src/ReactDebugHooks.js` only accepts `FunctionComponent`, `SimpleMemoComponent`, and `ForwardRef` fibers, and throws `Unknown Fiber. Needs to be a function component to inspect hooks.` for anything else.

That guard rejects `MemoComponent` fibers, which `getChangeDescription` passes in whenever the memoized component is *not* a "simple" function component — e.g. `memo(forwardRef(fn))` or `memo(fn)` where `fn` has statics like `defaultProps`. For those, the memo fiber is a pure wrapper: the reconciler always renders the resolved function on the **child** fiber, so the hooks live on the child, never on the wrapper.

Result: profiling a `memo(forwardRef(...))` component that re-renders with hooks in use surfaces the instrumentation error:

```
React instrumentation encountered an error:
Error: Unknown Fiber. Needs to be a function component to inspect hooks.
    at inspectHooksOfFiberImpl (installHook.js)
    ...
    at recordProfilingDurations (installHook.js)
```

and no change description is recorded for that component.

## The fix

In `inspectHooksOfFiberImpl`, resolve `MemoComponent` wrappers through their child fiber before the tag check (looping to also handle nested `memo(memo(...))`). The rest of the function then operates on the fiber that actually owns the hooks, exactly as it already does for `SimpleMemoComponent` (where the fiber *is* the function component).

This fixes every caller of `inspectHooksOfFiber` / `inspectHooksOfFiberWithoutDefaultDispatcher` at once (the DevTools profiler, `react-devtools-facade`, and any app that compiles debug hooks in), not just the change-description path.

## How did you test this change?

Added a regression test in `packages/react-devtools-shared/src/__tests__/profilerChangeDescriptions-test.js` (same harness as the existing change-description tests): a `memo(forwardRef(fn))` component that uses `useState`/`useMemo`, re-rendered with a changed prop while profiling with `recordChangeDescriptions: true`.

Verification:

- **Before the fix** (fix temporarily reverted, rebuilt): the new test fails with exactly the reported error — `Unknown Fiber. Needs to be a function component to inspect hooks.` thrown from `inspectHooksOfFiberImpl` during the commit callback, and no change description recorded.
- **After the fix** (rebuilt): `2 passed, 2 total`, and the change description snapshot confirms the component's render is now recorded:
  ```
  { "context": false, "didHooksChange": false, "hooks": [],
    "isFirstMount": false, "props": ["value"], "state": null }
  ```
- **No regressions**: ran the entire DevTools test project (`yarn jest --build --project devtools --release-channel=experimental`) on both clean `main` and with the fix: identical results — the same 11 suites / 42 tests fail in both runs (pre-existing failures in this environment, unrelated to this change), and with the fix one additional test (the new one) passes.
- Source-level `yarn test ReactHooksInspection` (react-debug-tools suites): `37 passed, 37 total`.
- `yarn prettier`, `yarn linc` (lint on changed files), and Flow (`dom-node` renderer): all clean.

title: [DOM] Attach the document-level selectionchange listener when the root is the document
body:
## Summary

Fixes #37695.

`listenToAllSupportedEvents` in `DOMPluginEventSystem.js` uses a single `listeningMarker` for two different purposes:

1. "this root container already has its delegated event listeners" (set on the root container), and
2. "this document already has the `selectionchange` listener" (set on `ownerDocument`).

That single marker conflates the two cases when the root container **is** the document (as done by `createRoot(document)` / `hydrateRoot(document, ...)` in Next.js App Router):

- **Bug 1 — `selectionchange` is never attached for a document root.** When the root is the document, the marker is set on the document *before* the `selectionchange` dedup check runs, so the check sees the marker and skips attaching the listener. Text inputs under a document root therefore never fire `onSelect` for selection changes that only arrive via `selectionchange` (e.g. `input.setSelectionRange(...)` from code, or dragging selection handles on a phone). The same input under a normal `div` root works.
- **Bug 2 — a document root created after any element root gets *no* listeners at all.** The first element root sets the marker on the document (for `selectionchange`); a later `createRoot(document)` then sees the marker on the document and skips attaching *all* of its delegated listeners — clicks stop working in the document root.

## The fix

Give the `selectionchange` dedup its own marker (`selectionChangeListeningMarker`) so the two purposes no longer interfere. Each element/document root still dedupes its own delegated listeners via `listeningMarker`, and the document-level `selectionchange` listener is attached exactly once regardless of root creation order.

## How did you test this change?

Added two regression tests in `packages/react-dom/src/__tests__/ReactDOMEventListener-test.js`, following the existing `should not subscribe to selectionchange twice` test pattern:

1. **`should subscribe to selectionchange when the root is the document`** — creates a root with `document` as the container and asserts the document receives exactly one `selectionchange` listener (`[false]`).
2. **`should not skip listeners on a document root if an element root was created first`** — creates a `div` root and renders, then creates a document root and renders a button; asserts the button's `onClick` actually fires via `simulateEventDispatch`, and that `selectionchange` was attached exactly once in total.

Verification:

- **Before the fix** (fix temporarily reverted, tests kept): both new tests fail (`2 failed, 23 passed`) — test 1 sees zero `selectionchange` listeners and test 2's click never fires.
- **After the fix**: the full suite passes — `yarn test ReactDOMEventListener` → `25 passed, 25 total`.
- No regressions in the wider event area (dev): `yarn test "ReactDOMEventListener|SelectEventPlugin|ChangeEventPlugin|SimpleEvents|ReactDOMSelection|ReactDOMTextarea|ReactDOMInput"` → `232 passed, 232 total`.
- Production build: `yarn test --prod "ReactDOMEventListener|SelectEventPlugin|ChangeEventPlugin"` → `53 passed, 53 total`.
- `yarn prettier`, `yarn linc` (lint on changed files) — clean.
- Flow: `No errors!` for both the `dom-node` and `dom-browser` renderer configs.

title: Type host config capability flags as boolean

labels.name: React Core Team
labels.description: Opened by a member of the React Core Team

body:
The reconciler is type checked once per renderer. In renderers that don't support a capability, its flag is exported as a literal (e.g. `supportsHydration = false` in ReactFiberConfigWithNoHydration), so Flow infers a literal type and reports every check of it as a constant condition. That's a property of one build, not of the shared code, which works with either value. We were suppressing it with `$FlowFixMe[constant-condition]` at each use.

Annotate the flag exports as `boolean` instead, so Flow treats them as unknown, and remove the 96 suppressions this makes unnecessary. Dead code elimination is unaffected, because the bundler still sees the literal value.

title: [Flight] Guard __webpack_get_script_filename__ in webpack client debug info
body:
## Summary

In runtimes that emulate Webpack client globals without `__webpack_get_script_filename__` (like Metro / React Native in Expo RSC setups), `addChunkDebugInfo` threw a `ReferenceError` during development when loading client components.

This checks that `__webpack_get_script_filename__` is actually a function before invoking it, and falls back to `__webpack_require__.u(chunkId)` or the metadata filename. Also handles environments where `document` is undefined.

Fixes #37038

## How did you test this change?

- Added a test in `ReactFlightDOMBrowser-test.js` where `__webpack_get_script_filename__` is undefined, verifying client components resolve and debug info attaches without throwing.
- Confirmed the test fails with `ReferenceError: __webpack_get_script_filename__ is not defined` without this change.
- `yarn test ReactFlightDOMBrowser-test.js`
- `yarn flow dom-browser`
- `yarn linc`
- `yarn prettier-check`

title: [Flight] Fix reviving errors without stack frames in debug info
body:
## Summary

`serializeDebugErrorValue` outlines the error info with `objectLimit: stack.length * 2 + 1`, but the error info object itself uses one from that budget. With zero frames the limit is 1, so the empty `stack` array gets deferred and goes out as `"$Y"`. The client then gets a string placeholder where it expects an array, `buildFakeCallStack` throws on it, and the error fails to revive. For an `AggregateError` that failure leaves `errors` as `null`, so `AggregateError(null, ...)` throws during parsing and the root never resolves.

Errors from Node internals (like the `ECONNREFUSED` from happy eyeballs in the issue) have no frames, so they hit this when they show up as a rejected I/O value or in a replayed log. Bumping the limit by one leaves room for the stack array itself.

Fixes #37728

## How did you test this change?

- Added a test that logs an `AggregateError` wrapping a frameless error and checks that it gets replayed. It fails on main (the log is never replayed) and passes with the fix.
- Ran the repro from the issue against 19.3.0 with the same one-line change applied to the published server bundle: the root now resolves to `"handled: all failed"` instead of throwing `object null is not iterable`.
- `yarn test packages/react-client packages/react-server packages/react-server-dom-webpack`. The only failure, `ReactFlightDOMEdge › should break up large sync components...`, also fails on main locally.
